section.title: Jesus by the Sea and the Restoration of Peter
section.sectionRationale: The Gospel's epilogue. By the Sea of Galilee the risen Jesus meets seven disciples who have fished all night in vain, fills their nets at His word, and shares a breakfast He has prepared. Then, beside a charcoal fire like the one where Peter denied Him, Jesus gently restores him with a threefold question, love and commission answering the threefold denial, calls him to shepherd the flock and to follow even to death, and quietly corrects the disciples' curiosity about the future.
section.thesis: The risen Jesus provides for and restores His failing disciples, filling the empty nets and, beside a charcoal fire, drawing from Peter a threefold confession of love that answers his threefold denial, recommissioning him to feed the flock and to follow to the death by which he will glorify God, so that the Gospel ends in grace, mission, and the call, follow Me.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the miraculous catch and the breakfast Jesus provides; the threefold restoration of Peter and his commission to feed the sheep; the foretelling of Peter's death and the call to follow; and the word about the beloved disciple and the Gospel's closing testimony.

verses.text: Later, by the Sea of Tiberias, Jesus again revealed Himself to the disciples. He made Himself known in this way:
Simon Peter, Thomas called Didymus, Nathanael from Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two other disciples were together.
Simon Peter told them, “I am going fishing.” “We will go with you,” they said. So they went out and got into the boat, but caught nothing that night.
Early in the morning, Jesus stood on the shore, but the disciples did not recognize that it was Jesus.
So He called out to them, “Children, do you have any fish?” “No,” they answered.
He told them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” So they cast it there, and they were unable to haul it in because of the great number of fish.
Then the disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It is the Lord!” As soon as Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment (for he had removed it) and jumped into the sea.
The other disciples came ashore in the boat. They dragged in the net full of fish, for they were not far from land, only about a hundred yards.
When they landed, they saw a charcoal fire there with fish on it, and some bread.
Jesus told them, “Bring some of the fish you have just caught.”
So Simon Peter went aboard and dragged the net ashore. It was full of large fish, 153, but even with so many, the net was not torn.
“Come, have breakfast,” Jesus said to them. None of the disciples dared to ask Him, “Who are You?” They knew it was the Lord.
Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and He did the same with the fish.
This was now the third time that Jesus appeared to the disciples after He was raised from the dead.

When they had finished eating, Jesus asked Simon Peter, “Simon son of John, do you {{agapao|love}} Me more than these?” “Yes, Lord,” he answered, “You know I {{phileo|love}} You.” Jesus replied, “Feed My lambs.”
Jesus asked a second time, “Simon son of John, do you love Me?” “Yes, Lord,” he answered, “You know I love You.” Jesus told him, “Shepherd My sheep.”

Jesus asked a third time, “Simon son of John, do you love Me?” Peter was deeply hurt that Jesus had asked him a third time, “Do you love Me?” “Lord, You know all things,” he replied. “You know I love You.” Jesus said to him, “Feed My sheep.

Truly, truly, I tell you, when you were young, you dressed yourself and walked where you wanted; but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and someone else will dress you and lead you where you do not want to go.”
Jesus said this to indicate the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God. And after He had said this, He told him, “{{akoloutheo|Follow Me}}.”
Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them. He was the one who had leaned back against Jesus at the supper to ask, “Lord, who is going to betray You?”
When Peter saw him, he asked, “Lord, what about him?”
Jesus answered, “If I want him to remain until I return, what is that to you? You follow Me!”

Because of this, the rumor spread among the brothers that this disciple would not die. However, Jesus did not say that he would not die, but only, “If I want him to remain until I return, what is that to you?”
This is the disciple who testifies to these things and who has written them down. And we know that his testimony is true.
There are many more things that Jesus did. If all of them were written down, I suppose that not even the world itself would have space for the books that would be written.

agapao.gloss: To love with self-giving, committed love. In His first two questions Jesus uses agapao, do you love Me, and Peter answers with phileo. Interpreters debate whether the shift between the two verbs is significant or simply stylistic variation, common in John. Either way, the threefold question of love graciously answers Peter's threefold denial and restores him.

phileo.gloss: To love with warm affection, the love of a friend. Peter answers each time with phileo, appealing to Jesus' knowledge of his heart, You know that I love You. Whether John intends a real distinction from agapao or a natural interchange of synonyms, Peter's insistence rests not on his own boasting but on the Lord who knows all things and knows his love.

akoloutheo.gloss: To follow, to accompany as a disciple. The Gospel that began with the call to follow ends with it: after restoring Peter and foretelling his death, Jesus simply says, follow Me. To follow is the essence of discipleship, a lifelong walking after Christ that will lead Peter even to a cross of his own, by which he will glorify God.

basic.context: The risen Jesus appears a third time to His disciples, by the Sea of Galilee. Peter and six others fish all night and catch nothing, until a figure on the shore tells them to cast on the other side, and the net fills. John recognizes Him: it is the Lord. On the shore Jesus has already made a charcoal fire and breakfast. After they eat, Jesus takes Peter aside and asks three times, do you love Me, matching Peter's three denials, and three times commissions him to feed His sheep. He foretells that Peter will one day die for Him and calls him, follow Me. When Peter asks about John, Jesus tells him to mind his own calling. The Gospel ends by affirming the truth of this eyewitness testimony.
basic.hermeneutics: This epilogue is about grace and recommissioning. The charcoal fire deliberately recalls the fire where Peter denied Jesus, and the threefold question answers the threefold denial. The key questions are, how does Jesus restore a failed disciple, and what does He call him to. He restores Peter not by ignoring the failure but by drawing out love and entrusting him with the flock. The debate over agapao and phileo should not overshadow the clear message: Peter is fully restored and commissioned, and the call is simply, follow Me.
basic.originalLanguages: The restoration turns on the verbs for love. Jesus asks with agapao, and Peter answers with phileo; the interplay, whether a real distinction or stylistic variation, frames a threefold confession of love. And the Gospel closes on the word it began with, akoloutheo, follow Me.
basic.typology: The miraculous catch of fish echoes the earlier call of the disciples to be fishers of people, now renewed for the mission ahead. The shepherd commission fulfills the pattern of Jesus the Good Shepherd entrusting under-shepherds with His flock. The charcoal fire answers the fire of denial with restoration.
basic.christ: Christ is the risen Lord who provides for His own, restores the fallen, and commissions them for service. He is the Good Shepherd who entrusts His sheep to Peter and calls him to follow even to death. He knows all things, including the love of a disciple who once failed.
basic.god: God is glorified in the faithful death of His servants, as Jesus says of Peter. The whole scene reveals a God who does not discard failures but restores and re-employs them, weaving even their falls into a deeper humility and love.
basic.crossReferences: Luke 5 tells the first miraculous catch and call. John 10 presents the Good Shepherd. John 18 recounts Peter's denial by a charcoal fire. 1 Peter 5 shows Peter later shepherding God's flock as he was commissioned.
basic.oneStory: The Gospel ends not with Peter's failure but with grace: the risen Christ restores the denier, entrusts him with the flock, and renews the call to follow. The story of Jesus flows on into the mission of His people, who feed His sheep and follow Him to the end, until He returns.

context.literary:
Chapter 21 is an epilogue, and John signals it as one. Chapter 20 ended with what reads like a closing statement of purpose, so the new chapter opens with a fresh introduction, 'Later, by the Sea of Tiberias, Jesus again revealed Himself,' verse 1. The verb translated 'revealed' (phaneroo) comes back in verse 14 as 'appeared,' and the two uses frame the whole fishing scene as a single manifestation. John also counts: this is 'now the third time,' verse 14, counting appearances to the disciples as a group, after 20:19 and 20:26.

Within the epilogue the scenes alternate between action and speech. The night of failure, the dawn word from the shore and the great catch occupy verses 1 to 8. Breakfast on the beach, verses 9 to 14, forms a quiet hinge, a meal made by the Lord. The dialogue with Peter, verses 15 to 19, is the heart. The last section, verses 20 to 25, turns to the beloved disciple and ends with two testimonies, verse 24 and 25.

Two details tie the chapter to the arrest night. The first is the charcoal fire, a word, anthrakia, that appears in the New Testament only at John 18:18 and here in verse 9. Peter warmed himself at one fire while he denied Jesus three times, John 18:18 and 18:25 to 27. He now smells another. The second is the net, which 'was not torn,' verse 11. The same verb, schizo, appears in John 19:24, where the soldiers say of the tunic, 'Let us not tear it.' John is fond of unbroken things, and the net that holds a great catch without tearing joins the seamless garment as a quiet picture of one undivided people.

The last verses return to the beloved disciple, whom Peter sees 'following,' verse 20, and the epilogue ends as the prologue began, with the claim that the book rests on testimony, 'we know that his testimony is true,' verse 24, as 19:35 also said.
context.historical:
The Sea of Tiberias is the Sea of Galilee under its Roman name. The city of Tiberias was founded by Herod Antipas on the western shore around the reign of Tiberius, and the lake took its name. John uses it also in John 6:1, so he writes with the Roman name in mind. The setting is the fishing economy of the lake, where families like Zebedee's ran boats with hired men, Mark 1:20, and fished at night with nets, since nets were worked in darkness or the cool of the early hours.

A night of fishing with nothing to show for it would be an ordinary disaster for a trade worker, and the miracle depends on the facts of that trade. The net is cast on the right side by a word from the shore. They were about a hundred yards away, which the BSB footnote converts from the Greek 'two hundred cubits.' The breakfast fire is a working man's meal, bread and fish, which is what the crowd also ate in John 6.

A shepherd's world lies behind verses 15 to 17. Israel's kings and leaders were called shepherds throughout the prophets, and Ezekiel 34 condemned shepherds who fed themselves. The call to 'feed' and 'shepherd' therefore recalled a long history of leadership failed and promised, and Jesus had already called Himself the Good Shepherd, John 10:11.

The prophecy of verse 18 reflects the manner of Roman executions. 'You will stretch out your hands' has been taken since the early centuries as a reference to crucifixion, and Christian tradition holds that Peter died as a martyr in Rome under Nero. The text of John states only that Peter would die in a way that glorifies God, and that is as far as it goes. The rumour in verse 23 shows that the first generation of believers was hearing and handling this kind of saying. They knew that the beloved disciple was long-lived and some drew a wrong conclusion.
context.canonical:
The chapter looks back at once to Luke 5:1 to 11, where Peter fished all night, caught nothing, and at the Lord's word let down the nets and broke them with fish. There Peter fell at Jesus' knees and said, 'Go away from me, Lord,' he said, 'for I am a sinful man.' Here the net holds, and Peter jumps in the water toward the Lord. The call 'from now on you will catch men,' Luke 5:10, is restored in a new form: now Peter is to feed and shepherd. The same Lord who first called him calls him again.

The threefold commission has deep roots in the Old Testament pictures of shepherding. Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34:11 to 16 present God as the shepherd who seeks, feeds and rescues the flock, and Ezekiel 34:23 promises a shepherd from David's line. Jesus in John 10 claims that role. In chapter 21 He shares it with Peter, not as a replacement, but as an under-shepherd. Peter later passes it on to elders, 'Be shepherds of God's flock that is among you,' 1 Peter 5:2, with the Chief Shepherd to appear, verse 4.

The call 'Follow Me' links the Gospel's beginning and end. Jesus says it to Philip in John 1:43, and in the farewell Peter is told he cannot follow now but will later, John 13:36. Verse 19 is where 'later' is spelled out. Paul, too, speaks of a death that glorifies God and of presenting the body as a living sacrifice, Romans 12:1, and Philippians 1:20 speaks of Christ being honoured in the body 'whether by life or by death.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wants the reader to learn two things from the final scene: that failure is not the last word in the kingdom, and that the real question of discipleship is love. The charcoal fire and the three questions are placed so that the reader cannot miss the correspondence. John gives no scene of Peter's repentance before this one. He lets the fire do the work. The healing is not in forgetting the denials but in matching each one with a confession.

The second aim is to settle a question the first generation was asking, which is what happened to the beloved disciple and what became of Peter. The question 'Lord, what about him?' in verse 21 is an old one for believers: why does one path look hard and another easy? Jesus' answer is a rebuke that is also a freedom, 'what is that to you? You follow Me!' John records it to correct a rumour, verse 23, and to show that Jesus never promised the author would live until He returned.

The final verses give the reader a framework for the whole book. John says he has chosen what to write, and that he has not claimed it is exhaustive, verse 25, with a hyperbole that his readers would have recognised as a way of saying that Jesus is larger than any account of Him.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The scene describes how the risen Lord dealt with one disciple. It does not command that every failure be restored by a threefold ritual of questions. What it prescribes by implication is the order: love comes first, service follows. The commission to feed His sheep was given to Peter in a personal setting. It is not an automatic title of office passed down to anyone who sits where he sat, and the New Testament itself treats the work of shepherding as shared among elders, Acts 20:28 and 1 Peter 5:1 to 4.

The prediction of Peter's death is a description of what would come, not a pattern that believers are told to expect for themselves. The phrase 'Follow Me' is the constant. What it means will vary: for Peter, a cross; for the beloved disciple, a long life of remembering. Verse 22 is a direct warning against measuring one's own calling against another person's.

The great catch is a sign of the Lord's provision and mission. It is not offered as a rule that obedience in work will always produce a full net.

debates.question: What does Jesus mean by 'more than these'?

views.label: More than these other disciples do
views.case: Peter had boasted that even if all fell away he would not, Matthew 26:33 and Mark 14:29. Jesus is testing that claim. The question presses on Peter's old comparison, and Peter's reply does not repeat it. He says only, 'You know I love You.'

views.label: More than you love these fish and boats
views.case: The disciples have just returned to their old trade. The 'these' may be the nets and the boat, and the question asks whether his first love is the fishing or the Lord. The scene is set among the tools of his former life, which he left once, Luke 5:11, and which he has now taken up again.

views.label: More than these other disciples love Me
views.case: Some read the sentence as asking Peter to measure his love against that of the others. It is the least natural of the three, since Peter could not know the others' hearts. The Greek of the phrase can carry more than one sense, so the sentence is truly open.

debates.bearing: On any of the three, the question presses beneath comparison to the heart. Peter's answer refuses to compare, and rests on the Lord's knowledge, 'You know I love You.'

debates.question: Is there a real difference between agapao and phileo in the exchange?

views.label: A deliberate step down
views.case: Jesus asks twice with agapao, a love of commitment, and Peter answers with phileo, a love of affection, so that on the third question Jesus comes down to Peter's word. Many preachers have built on this.

views.label: Stylistic variation
views.case: John uses the two verbs interchangeably elsewhere. The Father 'loves' the Son with agapao in 3:35 and with phileo in 5:20. Jesus is said to love Lazarus with phileo in 11:3 and with agapao in 11:5. The beloved disciple is the one Jesus loved by agapao in 13:23 and by phileo in 20:2. John also varies other pairs in the same passage, such as the verbs for 'know,' oida and ginosko, in verse 17, and the words for 'sheep.'

debates.bearing: The shared evidence favours variation, and what matters is the pattern of three questions and three answers. Peter's tone at the third question, 'deeply hurt,' shows the weight of the repetition and not a change of vocabulary.

debates.question: Who wrote chapter 21?

views.label: The author of the rest of the Gospel
views.case: The chapter shares the Gospel's style and its themes of the sea, the fire and the beloved disciple, and the manuscripts that survive all contain it. Verse 24 says the disciple 'has written them down,' which suggests that the same hand is behind it.

views.label: A later addition by the author's circle
views.case: The conclusion at 20:30 and 31 reads like an ending, and verse 24 shifts to 'we know that his testimony is true.' Some therefore see an editorial note by disciples who completed or arranged the book after the beloved disciple's death.

debates.bearing: Both views accept the chapter as part of the Gospel from the earliest manuscripts, and both say the testimony comes from the beloved disciple. The question does not change what the chapter teaches.

study.originalLanguages:
The questions of verses 15 to 17 are one of the best known puzzles in the Gospel. Jesus uses agapao in the first two, and in the third he uses phileo. Peter always answers with phileo. John elsewhere moves freely between the two verbs for the same love, so the exchange is better read as a repeated, deepening request for Peter's heart than as a graded test. The difference that is clear in the Greek is in the verbs of the commission, which change as well: 'Feed My lambs,' boske ta arnia, then 'Shepherd My sheep,' poimaine ta probata, then 'Feed My sheep.' The second uses poimaino, the whole work of shepherding, which includes guiding and guarding, and 1 Peter 5:2 later takes up the same verb.

'Do you love Me more than these?' uses a Greek construction that can be read in more than one way. The word 'these' could refer to people or things, and the text leaves the choice to the reader, which is why the debate above remains open.

In verse 7 the disciple whom Jesus loved says, 'It is the Lord!' and Peter 'put on his outer garment (for he had removed it).' The Greek says Peter was naked, gymnos, a word that can describe a man stripped to his working clothes. He dresses before diving in, which in the culture is a gesture of respect before the Lord. The detail fits the vividness of an eyewitness account.

In verse 5 Jesus calls out 'Children,' paidia, a warm form of address from the Master to men who have worked all night. In 21:18, 'you dressed yourself' translates a verb of girding, zonnymi, which is related to the verb John uses for Jesus tying the towel at the foot washing, John 13:4. The one who once girded Himself to serve now tells Peter someone else will gird him and lead him where he does not want to go.

Two words in verse 19 carry the whole sentence. 'The kind of death' uses the same phrase as John 12:33 and 18:32, where John used it to explain how Jesus Himself would die. And 'glorify,' doxazo, a key verb for the cross in John, is now applied to Peter's own death. 'Follow Me,' akoloutheo, is a present command, which carries the sense of keep following. It is the same word Jesus used at the start of the Gospel, John 1:43, and the one that ends Peter's story here, in verses 19 and 22.

The last word of the chapter is the world, kosmos, in the hyperbole of verse 25. John has counted what he wrote in verses 20:30 and 21:25 with signs and books, and in the end says that the world itself could not hold them.

typology.type: The great catch and the net of fishers of people
typology.fulfillment: In Luke 5:1 to 11 a night of empty nets ended with a catch that tore the nets and a commission, 'From now on you will catch men.' Here the same sequence reappears after the cross, and this time the net holds. The shift from a net that tears to a net that does not points to the Lord's work of gathering a people who are kept, which is the gospel's promise in John 10:28 and 17:12. The number 153 has no agreed meaning, and the interpretations are speculation. John's own point is that the catch was large, counted and unbroken. The type falls short only in that the mission to the nations is still in progress.

typology.type: The charcoal fires of denial and restoration
typology.fulfillment: The two fires are placed deliberately. At the first, Peter stood warming himself and said 'I am not,' John 18:25. At the second, the Lord has prepared the fire, and Peter is asked three times about his love. The structure is a re-enactment in which each denial is answered. This is not a type in the strict Old Testament sense but a narrative pattern, and it shows how Scripture's own shape heals memory.

Ezekiel 34 condemns shepherds who feed themselves, and God declares that He Himself will search for His sheep and set one shepherd over them, Ezekiel 34:11 and 23. Jesus is that Shepherd, John 10:11, and in John 21 He appoints an under-shepherd with the words 'Feed My lambs,' 'Shepherd My sheep.' Peter is told to care for flock that belong to the Lord, 'My lambs,' 'My sheep,' so that his authority is entirely borrowed. Later he calls himself a fellow elder and points to the Chief Shepherd, 1 Peter 5:1 to 4. The type falls short because Peter will die and the flock stays His.

typology.type: The meal prepared on the shore
typology.fulfillment: The Lord who fed five thousand with bread and fish, John 6:11, now serves breakfast with the same two foods. In verse 13 He 'took the bread and gave it to them,' wording that recalls John 6:11. The scene is a foretaste of the table the Lord prepares, as in Psalm 23:5 and Luke 22:30, and of the wedding supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9. The type falls short in that this is a simple meal by a lake, while the final feast is the gathered people of every nation.

study.christ:
The first thing the chapter shows about Christ is that He is the one who feeds. He is on the shore before them, with the fire lit and the fish on the coals, and the breakfast is His. Disciples who spent a night producing nothing are met by a Lord who provides what they could not. It is the pattern of the whole Gospel: bread for the crowd, wine at a wedding, life for the dead. The risen Christ has not stopped giving.

He is also the Lord who knows. Peter's answer is 'Lord, You know all things,' verse 17, and the Gospel has already shown that Jesus knew what was in people, John 2:25, and knew who would betray Him, John 6:64. The restoration works only because the Lord reads the heart. Peter cannot prove his love by words after his denials; he can only appeal to the knowledge of the one he failed, and that is enough.

He is the Good Shepherd who gives His sheep to others to tend without ceasing to own them. Three times He says 'My.' The pastoral office in the church depends on that: those who feed His sheep do so as His servants. Peter's call to follow even to death also reveals Christ as the pioneer, since He walked the road first, John 10:11 and 10:17 and 18, and Peter follows His steps, 1 Peter 2:21.

Guard against forcing the passage. The chapter does not make Peter the foundation of a lasting office in this scene, and the number of fish is not a code. What it shows plainly is the character of the risen Christ: He seeks His failed friends, He asks for love before service, and His 'Follow Me' is spoken to Peter after the worst week of Peter's life. The Christ of John 21 is the same Christ of John 1, full of grace and truth.
study.god:
This is a scene about the God who restores. The Gospel gives the Father's love, the Son's obedience and the Spirit's ongoing work, and John 21 is a small picture of divine mercy in human terms: no scolding, no inquiry into the details of the fall, but a fire, a meal and a question. God does not cancel the memory of Peter's sin. He gives Peter a way to answer it. That reflects the character of the God who proclaims Himself 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness,' Exodus 34:6.

The chapter also shows God's sovereignty over the small things of work. The fish come at a word and the net is full. The Lord knows where the shoal is, and the hand that rules galaxies directs fishing nets. Nothing in Peter's ordinary working life is outside His care. At the same time, the sovereignty is not cold or remote: the Lord who commands the shoal also tends a fire with fish and bread upon it, and calls tired men to come and eat. Power and tenderness are the same God at work.

Verse 19 says Peter would glorify God by his death. Here God is glorified not only in miracles and in life but in the faithful end of one of His servants, a thought that stands behind Philippians 1:20 and 2 Timothy 4:6 to 8. The same God who restores also calls, and what He calls to may cost everything. Yet the call is addressed by the One who goes before.

Verse 22 is a lesson about divine freedom. 'If I want him to remain until I return, what is that to you?' The Lord assigns different paths to different disciples and does not owe anyone an account of the difference. Worship here involves accepting that God's wisdom in distributing callings is beyond comparison. It also teaches humility about the future: even Jesus' words about it were misunderstood by His own followers, and John corrects the rumour carefully.

crossReferences.note: The first catch happened on the same lake after a fruitless night. The nets began to break, Peter fell at Jesus' knees confessing sin, and he was told he would catch people. John 21 reverses the pattern: the net holds, Peter rushes toward the Lord, and the commission is renewed after a deeper failure.

Peter, with the others, stands at a charcoal fire in the courtyard of the high priest and is asked whether he is one of the disciples. The setting is chosen by John to echo in 21:9, so the reader is prepared to see the second fire as an answer to the first.

The second and third denials end with the rooster crowing. John 21 sets three questions beside three denials, and the Lord's tone is the opposite of accusation. The echo is part of the care taken by the narrator to show that the failure is faced and healed rather than skipped.

Jesus is the Good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep and who has other sheep to bring in, so that there will be one flock and one shepherd. John 21:15 to 17 gives the flock to Peter's care, as an under-shepherd serving the one Shepherd.

Peter declared he would lay down his life and was told that he would deny three times, but also that he would follow later. John 21:18 and 19 shows the later follow through: a death that would glorify God, and a word of the same call, 'Follow Me,' to a man who had failed.

God promises to search for His scattered sheep, to feed them and to bind up the injured. Jesus fulfils this in His own care for Peter. The prophecy also shows why feeding is the first duty of an under-shepherd: it is God's own work shared out to others.

Peter writes as a fellow elder and urges others to shepherd the flock, eagerly and without lording it over them, until the Chief Shepherd appears. It is the commission of John 21 remembered and passed on by the man who received it, in his own words.

John uses a nearly identical phrase about the death by which Jesus would die. Using the same expression about Peter in 21:19 links the disciple's death to the Lord's and presents it as sharing in the glory of the cross, not as an unrelated end.

The soldiers choose not to tear the seamless tunic. The word for tear is the same one used for the net in John 21:11. In both places something that holds together is preserved, an image of the unity of those gathered to Christ.

John states his purpose at the end of chapter 20 and then adds an epilogue. Verse 30 speaks of other signs not written in the book, and 21:25 closes the Gospel in the same vein, so the two endings bracket the final chapter and show that the author chose his material with care.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story is the story of a God who makes a family and then keeps it in spite of its failures. Adam hid, Abraham lied about his wife, Israel made a calf, David took another man's wife, and every time God returned to the guilty with a word of grace and a renewed task. Peter's story is a short version of that long pattern: a promised loyalty, a public collapse, and then a meal on the shore. The old question that began in the garden, 'Where are you?' Genesis 3:9, is answered here by the Lord who comes looking at dawn.

John 21 is also where the Gospel connects with the history of the church. The sheep that Peter feeds are the people Jesus called 'other sheep' in John 10:16. The net that is not torn is the church gathered from the nations. The charge to follow to death anticipates the pattern of Acts, in which witnesses give their lives, Acts 7:59 and 12:2, and in which Peter is ultimately taken where he would rather not go. The Spirit who was breathed on the disciples in chapter 20 is the strength by which Peter will feed the flock.

The story is moving toward its conclusion in Revelation, where the Lamb is the Shepherd, 'the Lamb in the center of the throne will be their shepherd,' Revelation 7:17. The Chief Shepherd who appears will bring a crown that will not fade, 1 Peter 5:4. The failures of the shepherds of Israel are finally answered by a Shepherd who does not fail, and who tells every follower along the way the one thing He told Peter on the shore: 'Follow Me.'

quiz.q: How do the disciples come to recognize Jesus on the shore?

options.text: After the miraculous catch of fish at His word, the beloved disciple says, it is the Lord.
options.note: Verses 6 and 7 show recognition dawning through the great catch.

options.text: They recognize Him at once by His appearance on the shore.
options.note: At first they did not recognize Him; it was the miraculous catch that revealed the Lord.

options.text: He announces His own name to them.
options.note: He does not name Himself; the sign of the catch leads to recognition.

options.text: They realize it is Jesus once the nets are filled.
options.note: True, but it omits that the beloved disciple names Him, it is the Lord.

quiz.q: Why does Jesus ask Peter three times, do you love Me?

options.text: To answer Peter's threefold denial with a threefold confession and restoration.
options.note: The three questions, beside a charcoal fire, deliberately match Peter's three denials.

options.text: Because Jesus was unsure of Peter's answer.
options.note: Jesus knows all things; the repetition is for Peter's restoration, not Jesus' information.

options.text: To test whether Peter was worthy to lead.
options.note: The threefold question is gracious restoration answering his threefold denial, not a test of worthiness or an act of shaming.

options.text: To draw out Peter's love and recommission him.
options.note: True, but it omits the pointed correspondence to his threefold denial.

quiz.q: What does Jesus commission Peter to do?

options.text: To feed and shepherd His lambs and sheep.
options.note: Each of the three exchanges ends with a charge to feed or shepherd the flock.

options.text: To lead the other disciples as their head.
options.note: Peter is given real leadership, but it is shepherding and feeding the flock in service, not lording it over others.

options.text: To return to fishing for a living.
options.note: The commission is to care for Christ's people, not to resume ordinary fishing.

options.text: To care for Christ's people.
options.note: True, but it does not capture the specific shepherding language, feed and tend the sheep.

quiz.q: How does Jesus respond when Peter asks about the beloved disciple's future?

options.text: He redirects Peter to his own calling, saying, what is that to you? You follow Me.
options.note: Verse 22 turns Peter from comparison back to his own discipleship.

options.text: He promises that the beloved disciple will never die.
options.note: This is the very rumor John corrects; Jesus only posed a hypothetical and redirected Peter to follow Him.

options.text: He rebukes the beloved disciple sharply.
options.note: The word is to Peter about minding his own calling, not a rebuke of John.

options.text: He tells Peter not to worry about others' paths.
options.note: True in effect, but it omits the direct command, you follow Me.

quiz.q: How does the Gospel of John conclude?

options.text: By affirming the beloved disciple's true testimony and noting that Jesus did far more than could ever be written.
options.note: Verses 24 and 25 attest the testimony and marvel at the boundless works of Jesus.

options.text: By claiming to record every deed Jesus ever did.
options.note: The opposite; it says the world could not contain the books of all He did.

options.text: By simply ending the story after a resurrection appearance.
options.note: It does end with a resurrection appearance, but it also affirms the testimony is true and marvels at Jesus' boundless works.

options.text: By pointing to the reliability of the eyewitness account.
options.note: True, but it omits the closing wonder at the inexhaustible works of Jesus.

questions: The disciples toiled all night and caught nothing until Jesus spoke. Where are you laboring in your own strength, and what would it mean to work at His word instead?
Jesus restored Peter beside a fire like the one where he failed. How does it comfort you that Christ meets us at the very place of our failure to restore us?
Peter's restoration flowed straight into a commission to feed the sheep. How might Christ be turning your own failures into a deeper, humbler usefulness?
Jesus told Peter to stop comparing his path to John's and simply follow. Where does comparison distract you from your own call to follow Christ?
The Gospel ends with follow Me. As you finish this study of John, what is the next step of following Jesus that He is placing before you?

translationNotes.note: The Sea of Tiberias is another name for the Sea of Galilee, as the BSB footnote notes; the disciples had returned to their home region.

Jesus' questions use agapao, and Peter answers with phileo; interpreters differ on whether the change is a meaningful distinction or stylistic variation common in John. The clear point is Peter's full threefold restoration.
Stretch out your hands and be led where you do not want to go indicates, John explains, the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God, understood as martyrdom.
The narrator corrects a false rumor that the beloved disciple would not die; Jesus posed only a hypothetical, a caution against building beliefs on misunderstood sayings.
